title: How an Op-Ed in Support of Football Divided Oberlin’s Campus
author: @NewYorker
content:
Short on writers and needing to fill pages last October, Ava Harvey did what any sports editor for a small newspaper would have done: she assigned herself a football story. But since Harvey, then a senior at Oberlin College, was writing for the Oberlin Review, covering football was a rather tricky proposition. Oberlin’s team, the Yeomen, had finished 1–9 each of the previous two seasons. When Harvey began working on her column, during the 2025 season, the team was already 0–4, almost halfway to its eventual record of 0–10. A story breaking down Oberlin’s next opponent seemed useless. A feature on the team’s defense wouldn’t work, either. In its season opener, a home game against Calvin University, Oberlin had allowed its opponent to score seventy-four points before the start of the fourth quarter.

The Review has a history of publishing big feelings about football, keeping with the Oberlin tradition of having big feelings about a lot of things. Harvey decided that she wanted to write something “a little more controversial.” Her take? The school and its students should support the team more.

Had she stopped there, with a spirited call to fill the bleachers at Dick Bailey Field, that would likely have been that. But Harvey did not stop there. She felt bad for her friends on the team, not just because of their dreadful record but because of what she saw as a stark divide between football players and the rest of the student body. In her article, “Put Your Mouth Where Your Money Is: Back Oberlin Football,” she argued that “the majority of students are, at best, indifferent—if not outright hostile—to the sport.” She also noted that “the homogenized coastal culture historically propagated by the school”—despite Oberlin’s campus being in northern Ohio—“alienates Midwest athletes seeking a sense of home.” (Harvey herself is from Lansing, Michigan, and is a diehard Lions fan.) She pointed out that, in recent years, Oberlin’s best offensive season came after its newest recruits were prevented from visiting campus owing to the coronavirus pandemic. This was no coincidence, she contended: “Why would players choose a school where they’re viewed, at best, as an oddity, and at worst, as fundamentally incompatible with the institution’s values?”

After the article ran, something weird happened: people at Oberlin began talking about the football team. Friends told her that in the dining hall, where copies of the Review are often scattered like birdseed, some students were trashing the column. Harvey even noticed a spike in views of her LinkedIn page. About a month later, the Review’s opinions page published two responses, each taking aim at her rationale. The first called Harvey’s perspective “audacious,” adding that “the real issue with the piece is that there is no issue.” The second referred to the “illogical nature of the cultural argument” Harvey had made. Harvey felt like persona non grata, the lady who wrote that football column. “It definitely provoked a response,” she said. “So I guess I got what I was looking for.”

Oberlin is a Division III school that, by N.C.A.A. rule, doesn’t offer athletic scholarships. But having a football team, even one that never wins, is a suck on resources. As the Yeomen continued losing games last year, the larger college-football machine kept humming at campuses across the country. Ohio State, fresh off winning a national title with a twenty-million-dollar payroll, kept on buying separation from most of its peers. Down South, L.S.U. fired a coach to whom it still owed more than fifty million dollars, and then the Louisiana governor joked—maybe?—about having President Donald Trump choose the next hire. A core American truth is that football is a reflection of wherever it exists. Oberlin, it turned out, is no different, no matter how much it might want to be.

The most obvious fragmentation at Oberlin, a school of three thousand or so students, is right there in the institution’s full name: Oberlin College and Conservatory. There’s the liberal-arts college, and then there’s the renowned music conservatory. But just as at any school, the students are then split into many more subcultures, starting with those in the co-ops—student-run living and dining communities that essentially stand in for Greek life. There are also the journalists, the athletes, and the kids who spend sunny days doing contact improv, which was invented at Oberlin, tangling their limbs in the grass outside the library. There’s the Luddite Club, which last fall used a seventy-year-old typewriter to make a poster denouncing the school’s decision to offer students ChatGPT and Google Gemini subscriptions. There’s even a Let’s Talk About Death Club, which, according to its founder, the senior Bee Herbstman, holds “a lot of meetings that are about . . . death.”

Students describe Oberlin as a kind of oasis, a place where high-school misfits can find a community of outsiders. They also know that Oberlin is an avatar for the über-progressive, mad-about-every-micro-aggression school, which makes it hard not to frame their experience in relation to public perception. “It’s totally portrayed as Fox News’ worst nightmare, and maybe it is,” Herbstman told me. “But it doesn’t feel like the only thing we talk about at Oberlin is gender or feminism.”

“It’s like if ‘Portlandia’ was turned down a few notches and everyone was twenty,” Viv Tullis, a senior history major, told me. And so, when it comes to athletes, the traditional social hierarchy is completely inverted, especially as compared with other, more sports-centric schools. Tullis recalled that, back at her high school in Boulder, Colorado, it felt like “athletes were in charge of everything and running the show.” At Oberlin, she said, “it feels like it’s totally the reverse. I guess that does raise certain questions of what it means to be totally socially inclusive.”

To explain Oberlin’s social scene, Tullis used the dance department’s biannual show, saying that it might include watching spoken word about a performer’s menstrual cycle, maybe while the performer rolls around the stage. Or, she said, “it’s Friday night, you’re, like, let’s go crazy, and then there’s just a guy with a bassoon in the corner.” Such jazz parties, I learned, are one of the few settings in which football players and non-athletes regularly mix outside Oberlin’s classrooms. If the football team has live jazz at a postgame party, Lucy Wadman, another senior, said that she will try to get there early to snag a good spot where she can hear the music clearly. She does not, however, attend the football games themselves, at least not since the home opener her freshman year.

Oberlin won that day, one of two victories while Wadman has been on campus. That night, the jazz party, she told me, was probably the biggest party of her first three years. “It was insane,” she said. “Nobody cared, obviously, but it was just something to celebrate.” It makes you wonder what the Review coverage would read like if the Yeomen would just win another game.

Oberlin is not without some real football history. The last team in Ohio to beat Ohio State? That would be Oberlin, a 7–6 win in 1921. The first coaching job for John Heisman, of college-football-trophy fame, in 1892? That would be Oberlin again. And the school Peyton Manning almost chose before committing to Tennessee, when every program in the country was fighting for him? O.K., that one wasn’t Oberlin, but you get the point.

Football at Oberlin has not always felt so oxymoronic. But the true tradition, no matter the era, is the debate about how—or whether—football fits into Oberlin’s culture. “It’s part of Oberlin folklore to think of athletics as a problem, in some way,” Sebastiaan Faber, a professor of Hispanic studies, told me. Faber has been at Oberlin since 1999 and is in his first semester advising the student paper. “I think if you would run through the archives of the Oberlin Review,” he said, “you would see on the op-ed page regularly the same kinds of pieces about how football should be abolished, then people saying, ‘No, no, the football players that I know are also really good musicians and they love to read novels.’ It’s a permanent battle.”

When Khalid McCalla, a member of the Oberlin class of 2021, was looking to play college football, Division I coaches told him that he was too slow for a running back and too small to play linebacker. He ended up as a linebacker—at Oberlin. At his freshman orientation, in 2017, someone told him that there were three distinct groups on campus: athletes, NARPs (non-athletic regular people), and Obies. Ask fifteen Obies to define the term and you might get fifteen different responses. One clean answer is anyone in a co-op. But, broadly, an Obie is more likely than the average student to say “sportsball” or “athletic-type person” to describe an athlete. They’re also more likely to walk around barefoot, or to participate in activities like jello wrestling, as many students did during a weekend music festival last spring.

McCalla wanted to bridge these social divides, which eventually led him to quit football to do more on campus. (He was unhappy with how little playing time he was getting, too.) Another Oberlin graduate told me that McCalla was like a translator between athletes and non-athletes. But McCalla felt that some friends looked at him sideways for being on the team in the first place, because they felt that sports were “tools of the patriarchy or tools of oppression,” he said.

Still, the biggest challenges are on the field, all to play for a team that attracts few fans and very little interest beyond fellow-athletes. During a game, each side has eleven players on the field at a time, but a team’s full roster is much larger: many Division I programs carry the maximum hundred and five members. Smaller schools typically have smaller rosters; Hiram College, Oberlin’s first opponent this season, has a roster of sixty-eight. This year’s Oberlin squad, meanwhile, has just forty-one players in total. To compensate for its small size, Oberlin has seventeen players listed on the college’s athletics site with multiple positions. At the team’s early-morning practices, many players flip between offense and defense to prepare for any situation, especially when there are even a few injuries. “It does become a safety issue at that point,” a former player who graduated recently said. “I think the school has the resources and the ability to focus on it if they wanted to. I definitely feel for those guys and the future players who are coming in.”

The recent grad floated slightly looser admissions standards for football as a possible solution. I can already see the Review editorial slamming that idea. Harvey’s column, she said, reflected complaints that she had heard from a number of players, which included similar frustrations about the lack of, well, players. But what she hammered most was how, in her view, Oberlin has failed to make football players feel welcome. She wanted to see if the reaction might reveal insecurities, a sort of trick play for the truth.

As for Oberlin’s athletic director and the football team’s head coach, both declined my interview requests through a school spokeswoman, who instead sent along a three-hundred-and-sixty-three-word statement (plus a list of recent highlights in men’s lacrosse, women’s softball, women’s tennis, and men’s tennis). The statement recognized the roster size and injuries as a challenge for football, mentioning that the team has access to a sports psychologist. “Oberlin has always been a place where students ask hard questions, challenge assumptions, and debate what our values mean in practice,” the statement read. “Athletics is no exception. We see the student discussion about football as part of that tradition.”

Ghulam Woolman’s parents like to tell a story about a hike that they took when he was six years old. The Woolmans were with family friends. At some point, the conversation turned to Tom Brady and the Patriots, and Woolman didn’t know who they were talking about. He asked them to explain, not realizing how absurd of a question that was for a kid growing up near Boston, Massachusetts, in the twenty-tens. “It was kind of like being a six-year-old Catholic and not knowing who the Pope was,” Woolman told me. “Like, how did I miss this?”

When it came time for college, Woolman wanted to go to a school in a big city. He instead wound up in a small town in Ohio, having been sold on Oberlin by a performance of “Dracula” he saw at the end of a campus visit. He started there last fall as a freshman. He planned to get involved in theatre, but he also wanted to write for the Review. When Harvey published her football column, Woolman read it, loathed it, and saw an opportunity. And then, like a seasoned writer, he waited a month before publishing a rebuttal. “Obviously, being a freshman, starting as a staff writer, wanting to go into the opinion side of things, part of me was maybe, like, Oh, you want to make a name for yourself,” he said. “I feel like responding to this would be like tapping into the campus Zeitgeist.”

In his column, “Oberlin Does Not Need to Change Culture for Football,” Woolman said that Harvey’s logic was “shamefully faulty.” But instead of calling to abolish the football team, he defended Oberlin as it is, framing football as just another campus activity, not particularly deserving of face paint and giant crowds. “There is widespread indifference to the sport, but football is not unique in this,” Woolman wrote. “The indifference to football is the same people feel to soccer, or field hockey, or someone’s DJ performance at The ’Sco, or my standup. People go to events if they have a personal connection or if they have a free night and their interest is piqued.”

Woolman, like Harvey, kept on swinging. He described Harvey’s column as a “broadside that mischaracterized campus life and failed to appreciate what makes our college special.” This was the tame version, too, after a friend read the first draft and told him to rein it in a bit. “I was, like, you know what? I probably really should,” Woolman said later. But if Harvey wanted to use football as a mirror for Oberlin’s flaws, then he wanted to smash it into a bunch of tiny pieces. “I think people in the newsroom were kind of excited,” Woolman said. “Like, ooh, it’s sort of like a family fight, a staff writer and an editor going at it.”

“Actually having the football team is the inclusive thing,” Woolman told me. “And we don’t need it to be good for it to be meaningful.” In a vacuum, this was an intuitive argument: the idea that, unlike most of higher education, Oberlin can field a team without bending to the country’s football obsession. And yet another core American truth is that being normal about football is just about impossible. Nationally, there is more spending and attention on the sport than ever. The Senate is in knots over a bill that would try to regulate college football’s billion-dollar economy. The N.F.L. is coming for the night before Thanksgiving, as if Sundays, Mondays, Thursdays, Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas, New Year’s Eve, and some Saturdays weren’t enough. But as Faber, the longtime Oberlin professor, put it to me, the school’s desired self-image is as a “special place with a special way of doing things.” Preaching indifference to football, however radical that is, played straight into this sensibility. And so the column got “really, really big,” Woolman said, remaining in the Review’s trending-stories bar for two or three weeks. “Which, you know, you try not to get an ego about these things, but it’s pretty cool to see it up there,” he said.

After the Review ran the second editorial panning her, Harvey considered writing a response to the responses. But then the season ended, and then there were midterms, and then the semester came to a close, resetting the discourse until the next football column appears. It might even be here soon: the Yeomen, looking to win for the first time since November 26, 2024, have their season opener on Saturday. It’s a home game. ♦

title: Your Smartwatch May Not be as Smart as You Think it is - Nautilus
content:
Smartwatches have soared in popularity in recent years, and now roughly 30-40 percent of American adults own one of them. More than serving as just a timepiece or a second screen for notifications, these watches promise to monitor a growing number of health metrics—from blood pressure to sweat loss. But how accurate are they really? 

Featured Video

Kinesiologists from the University of Michigan recently published a new framework to help users understand what, exactly, smartwatches are measuring. 

Read more: “The Pitfalls of AI Health Coaches”

If you take a peek under the hood of your average smartwatch, you’ll find a suite of sensors, including an accelerometer, a gyroscope, GPS, and a photoplethysmogram (or PPG, which uses light to detect blood volume). These sensors collect raw data (acceleration, angular velocity, location, and optical signal data), and the good news is, they’re pretty accurate. 

But this data is just the input to the smartwatch, what users (and would-be consumers) are most interested in are the outputs. According to the researchers, this is where things get fuzzy. That’s because the signal provided by the raw data gets filtered through a layer of proprietary algorithms that churn out metrics like heart rate, physical activity, sleep duration, etc. The more recent the model, the more exotic the metric (i.e., water loss during exercise). 

According to the team, the farther from the sensory data the outputs are, the less accurate they are. For example, metrics like heart rate, step count, and outdoor pace are much more reliable than metrics like calories burned, sleep stages, blood glucose, and hydration loss. These “metrics” are more like estimates. 

“People shouldn’t take these metrics at face value,” study author Adam Lepley said in a statement. “In many cases, these devices are better suited to tracking trends over time, rather than as precise laboratory measurements.”

And that’s an important point. While these more exotic metrics may not represent a one-to-one agreement with lab-grade measures, they’re still useful for tracking your own progress over time. (Of course, the algorithms that generate the metrics are proprietary so if you switch brands they’re not likely to match.) The researchers also stress that any higher level recommendations from your devices, like exercise recovery time, should be taken with a grain of salt. 

In other words, listen to your body. It might be smarter than your watch.

title: Play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score | Aeon Essays
content:
Our kids were playing Settlers of Catan over the holidays. Or rather, they weren’t. They’d rearranged the strategy game’s hexagonal tiles into an archipelago of islands that no rulebook recognises, imagined ‘bridges’ built from wood, brick and stone, and invented a purpose for the game about network connectivity that had nothing to do with earning points. They were not playing Catan. They were playing in Catan, using its materials as components to make a world the designers never imagined.

My first instinct was to reach for the rulebook and teach them how the game actually works. My next was to figure out how I could win. It took me a while to realise what I really needed to do: build up the courage to ask if I could sit in and build with them. That was the moment something shifted – not for the kids, who were already there, but for me: a 48-year-old professor sitting on the carpet, making islands and building bridges without a point in sight.

You can play a game or you can play in a game. When you follow the official rules, pursue the stated objective, and measure yourself against opponents or a scoring system, that’s competition: playing a game. The Greeks had a word for this kind of play: agôn, from the god who personified conflict, struggle and contest. But when my kids disassembled the board and turned it into a world, they were doing something older and stranger. They were engaged in what the French sociologist Roger Caillois, in his taxonomy Man, Play and Games (1958), called paidia: free, spontaneous, unstructured play. The kind with no winner, no score, and no optimisation. The kind of play that has almost no place in adult life and, arguably, the kind we need the most, especially now, when even our leisure comes with leaderboards.

The entire architecture of digital life – with its algorithmic feeds, frictionless production and the ambient expectation that we should be consuming or optimising at all times – nudges us towards chasing outputs rather than generating meaning. We track our sleep and score our calm. Fitness apps turn the morning run into a contest; meditation apps gamify stillness with streak counters; language apps award achievement badges for what used to be called curiosity. Even journaling apps nudge users toward consistency scores. The gamification of leisure has turned into work everything that used to exist as its counterpoint. Leisure has become a third shift with its own metrics, its own guilt, and its own sense of falling behind.

The philosopher C Thi Nguyen calls this ‘value capture’: the process by which a game’s simplified, legible values start to colonise the real-world activity the game was supposed to serve. Their power arises from the fact that games don’t just create worlds, but new visions of the good, telling players what to care about by virtue of what the game rewards through scores. When you’re doing Duolingo to maintain your streak, or when your place on the running app’s leaderboard replaces the reason you started running, that’s value capture. The metric ate the meaning.

The Dutch historian and cultural critic Johan Huizinga saw this coming almost a century ago. In Homo Ludens (1938), he argued that play is not marginal to civilisation but, rather, generative of it. For Huizinga, law, philosophy, poetry and war all emerge from play’s ‘magic circle’: the bounded space where ordinary rules are suspended and something else becomes possible. Huizinga worried that the play element had been declining in Western civilisation since the end of the 18th century, eroded by industrialisation and professionalisation. What he feared has now been fulfilled. It’s not that we killed play; we captured it and harnessed it to a productivity framework. Then we packaged and sold it for passive consumption. The magic circle was instrumentalised into a dopamine hit.

What’s missing is neither ‘fun’ nor ‘competition’. We have plenty of those and, to be clear, I’m a huge fan of both. I grew up playing soccer and skiing. In my teens and 20s, I was a serious rock climber. Later I evolved into a competitive ultramarathon runner and now have 50-plus races under my belt, thousands of miles on trails in my legs, and two age-group national titles to my name. Agôn is what I do on weekends. But it’s not where I find meaning, build community, or figure out who I am.

A large part of the trouble is that we’ve eliminated the conditions in which free play arises. Watch the subway car on any morning commute. Every head is bowed to a screen. Not working, not thinking, just filling the time. Candy Crush in the checkout line. Instagram between floors in the elevator. Mere seconds of unstructured time trigger panic, and our fingers reach unconsciously for our phones. But boredom isn’t a problem; rather, it’s the condition in which the mind, left alone, begins to play by itself, to wander, associate, drift toward the transitional space where unexpected connections assemble unbidden. Every moment that we fill with a screen forecloses the free play of the mind. We don’t just need different games. We need more nothing.

Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children

Caillois saw the full spectrum of play: from agôn (competition) and alea (chance), to mimicry (role-playing) and ilinx (vertigo and disorientation). All four types sit on a continuum between paidia (complete improvisation) and ludus (structured rules). However, contemporary game culture tends to collapse this entire spectrum into one narrow band: competition plus structure. We have no category (not in the App Store and not in our cultural vocabulary) for paidia without agôn: our culture has no home for free, exploratory, contemplative play that refuses to compete.

Of course, paidia still erupts wherever people stop keeping score: kids on a playground invent rules then abandon them mid-sentence, Minecraft’s creative mode hosts millions of players building dreamworlds for the sake of building; Lego, at its best, is a pure paidia portal – recombinatory, autotelic, improvisational. But these exceptions clarify the problem: Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children. It’s not that free play has vanished, it just exists under constant threat of value capture. We do it in spite of our platforms, not because of them.

Moreover, the kinds of play that refuse to compete or optimise, or produce a measurable outcome, lack cultural prestige and social infrastructure. The British psychoanalyst and paediatrician Donald W Winnicott would have recognised this absence as a clinical emergency. In Playing and Reality (1971), Winnicott argued that play is not what children do on the way to becoming productive adults; it is a crucial part of how human beings maintain their worlds. Through play we become present to our own experience, capable of surprise, alive to the difference between going through the motions and actually being there.

Winnicott’s key concept is transitional space, though ‘space’ is misleading here because he has in mind not a location but a condition. Think of a conversation so engrossing that you forget you’re speaking and say something you didn’t know you thought until you heard it leave your mouth. You’re not entirely inside your own head (fantasy) and you’re not entirely performing for an audience (compliance). You are in between. That in-between zone – neither fully private nor fully public, neither pure inner life nor pure external task – is what Winnicott called transitional space. It’s where creativity, art and what he called ‘imaginative living’ originate.

His most radical claim still hits like an urgent diagnosis: ‘It is creative apperception more than anything else that makes the individual feel that life is worth living.’ He contrasts this with compliance, a relationship to external reality that ‘carries with it a sense of futility’. It is worth pausing to unpack this fully. Winnicott is arguing that what makes life meaningful is ultimately not achieving goals, having a family or even making art. It’s about how we see the world. ‘Apperception’ names a mode of encounter in which perception is not passive reception but active engagement. The difference is subtle but decisive: in ordinary perception, the world is simply there and the self adjusts to it; in creative apperception, we co-create the world, forging something between self and environment in the zone of play.

Compliance, by contrast, is life lived on someone else’s terms, following scripts, bowing before scores and metrics: moving through a world already defined in advance. Nothing new is risked, nothing genuinely one’s own is made. Most people, Winnicott believed, experience just enough creativity to recognise its absence, sensing that they are mostly ‘living uncreatively, as if caught up in the creativity of someone else, or of a machine.’

That last sentence, written in 1971, strikes me as the most prescient insight from 20th-century psychology for our time. Long before the personal computer, before the algorithm, and before we voluntarily installed surveillance engines in our pockets and called them phones, Winnicott worried about being caught up in the creativity of a machine. He also had a solution: play. For Winnicott, play is the condition of feeling real on a daily basis.

Friedrich Schiller, writing almost two centuries before Winnicott, made the same case from the other direction. In On the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), he argued that human beings are torn between the pull of raw sensation and the push toward abstract order, and that only what he called the ‘play drive’ integrates both. It’s a bold claim. Schiller wrote that ‘man only plays when he is in the fullest sense of the word a human being, and he is only fully a human being when he plays.’ Winnicott tells you what play does psychologically: it makes life feel real. Schiller tells you what it does metaphysically: it makes you whole.

Simply put: adults need play as desperately as children do – a zone where inner life meets outer materiality and something unpredictable emerges. The Greeks, of course, had a term for this. Aristotle’s medieval fanboy Thomas Aquinas identified eutrapelia, the habit of knowing when and how to play well, as a genuine and discrete virtue. A person who never plays is as disordered as one who never works. I’m not talking about ‘work-life balance’, an exhausted metaphor that still treats play as recovery time for the next productive thing. To practise the virtue of eutrapelia means that a good life requires play. You don’t earn it. You practise it, daily.

The question, then, isn’t whether to play. It is where does the practice live, and how can we regain it in our daily lives, and valorise it in our culture.

For years, I’ve commuted on foot from Grand Central Station to 14th Street, 30 blocks, give or take. I told myself it was exercise, or that I was saving the subway fare, or that I liked the air. But the truth is I was thinking. Or rather, I was letting thinking happen. The lecture I couldn’t outline at my desk would assemble itself somewhere around 34th Street, the important points falling into sequence with my footfalls, the argument clarifying as if the motion itself were doing the editing. I wasn’t working on the lecture. I was walking in it, the way my kids were playing in Catan.

Walking increased the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems by 60 per cent

The experience is ancient and well-documented. Friedrich Nietzsche reputedly walked six to eight hours every day, and insisted in his Twilight of the Idols (1889) that ‘Only thoughts that come by walking have any value.’ Aristotle’s Lyceum was called the peripatetic school for its walkways (peripatoi). Jean-Jacques Rousseau claimed that he could compose only while walking. Albert Einstein walked from his home at Princeton, New Jersey to the Institute for Advanced Study and back each day, and supposedly told colleagues that the walk was where the real thinking happened; the office was where he wrote it down.

Contemporary research confirms these intuitions, this idea that walking is a form of play for the mind as well as the feet. In 2014, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz at Stanford University found that walking increased divergent thinking – the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems – by roughly 60 per cent. Curiously, a treadmill facing a blank wall worked nearly as well as wandering Stanford’s campus, suggesting that it’s the exercise, not the scenery, producing the results. Metronomic motion allows the thinking to arrive.

Push the body further and something stranger happens. Caillois’s taxonomy includes a category almost nobody talks about: ilinx, the play of vertigo and disorientation. Spinning until you’re dizzy. Or running past the point where the split times stop mattering and the self loosens its grip. I know this territory from the inside. The first question at the start of a 100-mile race isn’t whether your legs are ready. It’s whether your mind is: wanting to win might get you to the start-line of your local 5K, but agôn won’t get you to the finish of an ultra-marathon. And it’s a love of trails that makes those miles magical. Nguyen would call this striving play. The goal exists to make the experience of striving possible, not the other way around. The finish line is just the means; the journey is the destination.

Our son does something similar in our basement, though his materials are metal, wood and stone rather than miles of trail. He crafts with scraps of found steel, fixes electric motors, carves wooden animals, shapes copper into jewellery and stone into rings. Nobody assigned this. No tutorial dictates the sequence. The material teaches the craft: copper tells you what it wants to become; stone suggests a shape and you listen or it breaks. At the workbench, inner vision meets the friction of the physical world and something neither planned nor accidental emerges.

Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space, play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score

My son doesn’t sell what he makes. He gives it away: the knife to a friend, the carved animal to a teacher. Play pursued for its own sake, with no metric and no market, overflows into generosity precisely because nothing was extracted. When something beautiful emerges from a process that asked for nothing, the most natural thing in the world is to give it away. What he makes enters the world not as commodity but as gift.

I see the same dynamic at my day job, though, again, the materials are different. I’m a professor of literary studies, and the best sessions in my seminars have nothing to do with instruction. They obey the logic of improv: ‘yes, and’. A student notices something strange in a passage (a word that doesn’t fit, a silence where speech should be) and someone else picks it up, turns it over, connects it to something from three weeks ago, and suddenly the room is thinking a thought nobody walked in with. The seminar, at its best, builds transitional space inside an institution that mostly rewards compliance. It opens up the zone between private thought and public evaluation, where a student says something she didn’t know she believed until she heard it leave her mouth.

The same dynamic lives in a jazz combo finding a groove nobody charted, a graphic designer noodling with shapes until one surprises her, a group of friends kicking a ball around with no teams and no score. It lives in my son’s basement workshop and on the trail at mile eight, and in the 30-block walk where the lecture writes itself. Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space – where inner life meets outer material and something unpredictable emerges – play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score.

Aristotle thought that contemplation (theoria) was the highest human activity because it was done purely for its own sake, absorbing the entire human person. For centuries, and across domains of religion, the academy and the law, that hierarchy held, ranking the contemplative life above the active life, thinking above doing. But maybe the question itself is misleading. The question ‘What is the highest human activity?’ is itself a competition, an agôn. Play doesn’t enter that contest. Play dissolves it. Play is autotelic and relational, solitary and shared, serious and free; it refuses the binary.

Schiller, Huizinga and Winnicott were not wrong; play does makes life worth living. The capacity for play – the willingness to stop optimising, to sit on the floor, to walk without a destination, to make something and give it away – embraces a virtue with an old name: eutrapelia. It is the habit of playing well. The ordinary magic of being real.

title: Your Boss Is Watching You - Nautilus
content:
This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine.

Featured Video

Ready for a Whopper with a side of Orwell? Earlier this year, Burger King announced the rollout of Patty, an AI chatbot imbedded in headsets that tracks if cashiers neglect to say please and thank you and chimes in when a soda fountain is running low.

Advances in AI, cameras, sensors and tracking software have given employers unprecedented power to monitor employees. They now observe the physical location of workers, the length and content of phone calls, keystrokes per minute, and even the tone and pitch of conversations with customers.

Now, as companies search for new ways to watch their workforce, researchers are taking a close look at the consequences of constant surveillance.

Employee monitoring has become standard practice in multiple industries and workplaces. Drivers delivering packages or pizzas are increasingly being watched by AI-powered surveillance systems. Many employees in Amazon warehouses are continuously tracked through handheld scanners, badge swipes and workstation software.

Technologies that keep tabs on employees hold a strong appeal for corporate leadership, says Cornelius König, a psychology researcher at Saarland University in Germany. Leaders may believe that close surveillance can help identify top performers, increase efficiency or improve safety, he says.

In practice, though, such benefits are elusive. When König reviewed studies on employee monitoring in the 2025 issue of the Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, he found little to suggest that electronic surveillance improved performance. “My general take is that [monitoring] isn’t going to matter as much as employers assume,” he says.

Despite the lack of evidence, the global market for employee-monitoring technology is expected to exceed $4 billion in 2026, largely due to major companies in North America. A New York Times investigation in 2022 found that eight out of the 10 largest private US employers, including United Parcel Service, Amazon and UnitedHealth Group, tracked productivity metrics of individual workers, often in real time.

US postal workers are also closely watched. Delivering mail “feels less like public service and more like working inside a quiet surveillance state,” said a Reddit user in 2025. “We’re tracked down to the second. Every scan. Every step. Every stop. They monitor our GPS in real time. They can pull up on us unannounced. We get questioned for things as human as needing the restroom or checking a package twice.”

Any employer of any size can get into the monitoring business. Amazon Web Services sells thousands and thousands of software programs for employee monitoring, says Michele Molè, an employment law researcher at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. Adding a monitoring app to the workplace can be as easy as downloading Spotify, he says. But instead of music, employers get a stream of data about how each employee is behaving every minute of their day.

Companies that hope to increase their workforce’s performance through monitoring face a basic obstacle in human nature, König says. Workers might briefly up their game, but they tend to revert to their normal routines. “They become habituated,” he says. In his review, he pointed to growing evidence that even body cameras worn by police — an especially high-profile, high-stakes example of surveillance — don’t significantly change the behavior of either the police or the public over the long term.

When workers do respond to monitoring, there can be unintended consequences. A 2020 study found that electronically monitored truck drivers were less likely to exceed daily limits for driving hours, but they also were more likely to crash.

König is far from the only skeptic. “There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance,” says Daniel Ravid, a management researcher at the University of New Mexico.

Ravid conducted a 2022 meta-analysis that combined the results of studies involving more than 23,000 subjects in laboratory experiments and workplace settings, including workers in call centers and offices and police on patrol. Taken together, the studies found no correlation between levels of monitoring and employee performance.

That’s partly because some employees find workarounds to monitoring, even if that means tapping their keyboard periodically while they’re reading a book at lunch. “People are incredibly creative and adaptable, and they’ll find ways to reassert their freedom when it’s threatened or taken away,” Ravid says.

Ravid’s meta-analysis found that any type of monitoring — subtle or obvious, incidental or invasive — tended to increase workplace stress. “I think anything that undermines a sense of dignity is also going to undermine employee attitudes,” he says.

A 2024 study of more than 3,500 workers in Canada underscored the potential downsides of monitoring: Employees who perceived that they were being surveilled on the job reported that they felt more pressure and stress and less autonomy and privacy at work.

In an age of “datafication,” it’s not surprising that companies would look for new metrics to evaluate employees, says Kirstie Ball, a management researcher at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. “The systematic gathering of data about people and what they’re doing is part and parcel of modernity,” she says. “Surveillance becomes a means of getting things done.”

But not every company knows how to make good use of all those data points, Ball says. “There are many pitfalls along the way. Are you measuring what you think you’re measuring? Are you interpreting the data correctly according to the purpose that you gathered it, or are you looking at it just because you can?”

Employee surveillance without any coherent plan to use the data has become a commonplace scenario in modern companies, König says. Many workplaces end up collecting data simply because they have the technology, not because surveillance supports the company’s overall business strategy. “They end up with terabytes of data on a drive somewhere but don’t know what to do with it.”

Modern surveillance is an inherently electronic exercise, but companies can’t just install an app and expect results, Ravid says. “If managers think that they have a perfect way to measure performance because they have advanced technologies, they’re wrong,” he says. “They still need human insight and conversations to contextualize that data.”

Laws protecting employees from overly invasive surveillance generally haven’t kept pace with technology, says Molè, who wrote the 2026 book Monitored at Work. While the European Union has strong employee privacy laws, with additional legal protections in nations like Italy, Spain, France and Germany, workers in the US have far fewer safeguards and are more likely to be placed under a microscope.

In 2023, three current or former Amazon delivery drivers in Colorado filed a class action lawsuit against Amazon claiming that they were under excessive AI-assisted surveillance and that delivery quotas made it difficult to take necessary breaks. “The drivers were forced to pee in bottles,” Molè says. “This is not happening in Europe.” Amazon called for arbitration, noting that drivers work directly for outside delivery service providers who have contracts with the multitrillion-dollar company, not Amazon itself. The case is ongoing.

Other legal issues can lurk in the fine print that comes with monitoring software. Bosses who download monitoring apps they can’t customize are essentially letting outside companies take control of their employees’ data with little oversight or knowledge of how the data could be used. “We need more labor laws that target providers of technologies,” Molè says. Surveillance companies should be required to work directly with companies and their employees to clearly explain the technologies and tailor each product to meet specific needs and reach specific goals, he says.

Theoretically, monitoring could be a part of a healthy company culture that encourages success, Molè says. “People under monitoring should have a sense of being valued, and the monitoring should be truly meaningful for improving everyone’s working conditions and methods,” he says. “Good monitoring is based on mutual trust.” Companies that thoughtfully build their own system for tracking employee outputs instead of superimposing some “creepy and odd” tool found online are more likely to see actual benefits, he adds.

Success is certainly possible. Headbands that track brainwaves may seem invasive, but an Australian mining company found that such technology helped reduce fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. A 2024 study of remote workers on Upwork found that the productivity of top-performing workers dropped nearly 20 percent after they were allowed to turn off monitoring software without explanation, suggesting that the software had some benefits.

But productivity didn’t fall when that high-performing group was told they had the opportunity to go without supervision because of their impressive output, underscoring the importance of good management — leading the researchers to conclude that spending money on good managers could yield better results than spending it on monitoring software.

Transparency can go a long way to improving workplace culture, Ravid says. His meta-analysis found that, compared with workers who are surveilled without much explanation or consent, workers who have a clear understanding of how they are being monitored and how the data will be used also have a greater sense of fairness and job satisfaction.

New technologies will continue to join the ranks of Burger King’s Patty and other monitoring devices in the modern workforce. But if companies don’t change their basic approach, the results will likely be the be the same: suspicion and confusion for employees and few tangible benefits for employers.

This article originally appeared in Knowable Magazine, a nonprofit publication dedicated to making scientific knowledge accessible to all. Sign up for Knowable Magazine’s newsletter.

title: I have filled GTA 5 with realistic Los Angeles snow
author: Joshua Wolens
content:
Los Santos Customs

I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

Okay, two things. First: Los Santos Customs will be taking a hiatus next week, as I spend nine days in a row sleeping and attempting to develop the antibodies to counter whatever exotic German illness it is I acquired at Gamescom 2026.

Second: it's snowing in Los Santos, just like the real-life LA.

I have installed WinterV Beta, with the aim of making Grand Theft Auto 5's weather a little more interesting than it usually is. The pitch is simple: what if there was snow? Well, reader, having played a little GTA 5 with WinterV Beta, I can assure you that there very much is snow. Plus, all the world's lighting takes on a kind of a sickly, ochre hue, which is also just like LA.

From the sky: flurries of flakes. On the roads: cars covered in a sheen of powder, tyre-chains inexplicably equipped (the snow does not, in my version of GTA 5 where a significant chunk of the exterior map has absconded to the phantom zone, settle). In the air: a crisp winter chill. Santa Claus is coming to town; fire a truck at him.

I can't tell you if the presence of snow on the city roads impacts car handling because, as we have established, cars in my GTA 5 no longer have handling. Nevertheless, it does change the vibe quite a lot. As someone who's spent a lot of the last month looking at GTA 5—a change is as good as a rest.

But also, it is time for a rest. I will see you the week after next, whereupon we'll probably finally convert this game into GTA 6. I can feel it.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

One of Josh's first memories is of playing Quake 2 on the family computer when he was much too young to be doing that, and he's been irreparably game-brained ever since. His writing has been featured in Vice, Fanbyte, and the Financial Times. He'll play pretty much anything, and has written far too much on everything from visual novels to Assassin's Creed. His most profound loves are for CRPGs, immersive sims, and any game whose ambition outstrips its budget. He thinks you're all far too mean about Deus Ex: Invisible War.

title: Next week, for the first time ever, Nintendo is hosting two Directs back-to-back - and the first one is dedicated to The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
Direct action.

Back in June, we learned that we're officially getting a The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, which is supposedly coming to Switch 2 later this year (and we first heard rumours about it back in March). But, as we approach the latter quarter of the year, we still don't know much about this remake, what it looks like, how it plays, or... well, anything really.

Enter next week's Nintendo Direct. Nintendo has announced it will livestream a special, dedicated The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct next week, wihch will be followed by a second, more general Nintendo Direct.

The Zelda presentation will take place on September 8 at 7am PT / 10am ET / 3pm BST and last about 30 minutes. As its name suggests, the Zelda Direct will share information about how Nintendo plans to commemorate the Zelda series’ 40th anniversary. Will we finally see a trailer for the Legend of Zelda movie?

The Zelda presentation takes place on 8th September at 3pm BST, 7am PT, and 10am ET. It's set to last about 30 minutes. We will certainly get more news on Ocarina here, but I'd also expect to see some other tidbits from Zelda as Nintendo pulls back the curtain on what to expect for the big anniversary celebration.

The next day, 9th September, a general Nintendo Direct will take place on at 3pm BST, 7am PT and 10am ET. This one is going to take 45 minutes, and will be specifically aimed at Nintendo Switch 2 games coming this winter. There'll be a Nintendo Treehouse: Live session afterwards that last nearly two hours (110 minutes).

Two full Direct streams in one week, and then nearly two hours of Treehouse? Yes, that is unprecedented - this is the first time Nintendo has ever run this much new info back-to-back.

title: 'There is absolutely no generative AI in Space Marine 3' promises Saber Interactive executive
author: Ted Litchfield
content:
In a Gamescom interview with IGN, Saber CCO and former id Software dev Tim Willits said that the company's upcoming Space Marine follow-up is not using generative AI in its development. The studio has otherwise been embracing the technology, which was at the heart of the recent Rideshare Stimulator controversy.

"There is absolutely no generative AI in Space Marine 3 or Hellraiser or Stuntman or Turok or Jurassic Park, or [Saber's John Wick game]," Willits told IGN. "But like we said, we're going to experiment with it. Try it out in Rideshare, see if it works. See if people like it. If they don't like it, we're like, 'All right.'"

It seems that Saber is far more circumspect about using generative AI in its big ticket games, especially when there are license holders like Lionsgate or Paramount to consider.

Warhammer 40K owner Games Workshop, for its part, is enforcing strict internal rules against genAI use in any of its products or advertising, a crowd-pleasing stance that contrasts with rival tabletop giant Wizards of the Coast's willingness to play footsie with AI usage.

But Willits, like Saber CEO Matt Karch, is solidly pro-AI, and sees smaller projects like Rideshare Stimulator as an opportunity to feel it out. "If you're going to experiment, it's a good one to experiment on," Willits said. "If anyone tells you that they have it figured out, they don't. It'll take a couple years and things will settle out and we'll figure it out."

PCG news writer Joshua Wolens had his own conversation with Willits at Gamescom, and touched on similar topics. Willits believes that team size and overspecialization are major contributing factors to the industry's current economic crisis, but also argues that this crisis isn't as bad as it's being presented. Willits also said that, had the OG id Software crew gotten their hands on generative AI back in the day, they would have aggressively used it.

Ted has been thinking about PC games and bothering anyone who would listen with his thoughts on them ever since he booted up his sister's copy of Neverwinter Nights on the family computer. title: UN experts call on Honduras to halt evictions of peasant, Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities
content:
News

UN experts call on Honduras to halt evictions of peasant, Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities

A group of UN experts called on Honduras Friday to immediately halt evictions of peasant, Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities taking place under Decree No. 107-2026, also known as the Law for the Strengthening and Protection of the Agro-Industrial Sector, Energy Projects, Tourism, Livestock, and Small Agricultural Producers.

The experts wrote: “We cannot stand by and watch the deliberate closing of every legal door through which a peasant, Indigenous or Afro-descendant family in Honduras can challenge dispossession.” The decree declares specified projects to be of national interest, expedites administrative procedures, and directs authorities to act against occupations and blockades. It states that it does not apply in recognized Indigenous territories without free, prior and informed consultation. The experts nevertheless argued that the law could allow companies to obtain land cultivated by cooperatives and local farmers without agrarian review or adequate consideration of ancestral territorial claims.

The experts also warned that the decree could conflict with Honduras’ obligation to respect, protect, and fulfill the right to food. They said dispossessing communities of land essential to their food security would undermine access to productive resources.

They especially condemned evictions carried out by Honduran authorities on July 6, including an operation affecting the Garífuna community of San Juan in Tela. According to Amnesty International, five members of the Black Fraternal Organization of Honduras were arrested during the operation and now face charges of aggravated usurpation related to their defense of the community’s ancestral territory. The operation followed a 2023 judgment in which the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Honduras responsible for failing to guarantee the San Juan community’s collective-property and related rights and ordered the state to take measures to title, delimit, and demarcate territory for the community and provide other reparations.

The experts urged the Honduran government to halt any further evictions and consult affected communities on outstanding land claims before proceeding with additional eviction orders. They also called on authorities to investigate violence against the Garífuna community and urged companies involved in business activities in Honduras to implement human rights due diligence and prevent and mitigate risks to local communities and human rights defenders.

title: An Essay on How to Get Top Grades On Law School Exams
author: OrinKerr
content:
Back in 2007, here at the Volokh Conspiracy, I had a post on how to excel on law school exams.  I have heard that the post is still read among law students, so I decided to expand on that post and turn it into a more helpful essay for today's students to read.

I finally finished the draft, and I posted it on SSRN yesterday.  You can read it here:  How to Excel on Law School Essay Exams: A Guide for Students.  It begins:

This Essay offers guidance on how law students can earn high grades on law school essay exams. It starts with the goals law professors have when writing exams, which then frames what counts as a poor or strong performance. The essay then presents a hypothetical exam question with four answers, and it grades the answers to help explain what makes the different answers better or worse.

This is just a first draft, and I plan to improve it over the semester, so please send specific suggestions for improvement to me at okerr at law dot standord dot edu.  I'm particularly interested in feedback from other law professors, as I'm trying to capture how grading looks from the faculty perspective, all to help students do their best.

I see this essay as a companion piece to my 2007 essay, How to Read a Legal Opinion: A Guide for New Law Students, and also last year's video, So You're About to Start Law School: A Guide to the First Month.  The goal of all three has been to share the insider knowledge that connected people have with everyone else, so that students without connections start off on more equal footing and law school on the whole is more fair.

title: Mail-in voting returns to the interim docket
author: Nora Collins
content:
Skip to main content

Newsletter

Sep 4, 2026

There will be no SCOTUStoday newsletter on Monday in recognition of the Labor Day holiday. We’ll be back in your inboxes on Tuesday. Enjoy the weekend!

If you are interested in attending The SCOTUSblog Summit: 2026 Term Preview on Wednesday, Sept. 16, in Washington, D.C., don’t forget to fill out this registration request.

At the Court

On Thursday, the Trump administration urged the Supreme Court to temporarily pause an order blocking the government from implementing parts of a U.S. Postal Service rule on mail-in ballots. For more on the new interim docket request, see the On Site section below.

Today at 9:30 a.m. EDT, the court will release its third and final summer order list. (We discussed what these lists typically address in our July 13 newsletter.)

Two Republican groups asked the court on its interim docket to block a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit preventing political parties and joint fundraising committees from paying preferential broadcast rates for political ads. On Thursday, the Democratic candidates who challenged the groups’ access to the lower rates urged the court to leave the 4th Circuit’s ruling in place. For more on the filing, see the On Site section.

In another interim docket dispute, a Michigan group asked the court to require Michigan election officials to put on the November ballot its proposal for requiring proof of citizenship to vote in the state. On Thursday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied that request. Learn more about the dispute in the Morning Reads section.

Morning Reads

Supreme Court refuses to put proof-of-citizenship amendment on Michigan ballot

Kelsey Reichmann, Courthouse News Service

On Thursday, the Supreme Court declined “to take emergency action ... to put a proof-of-citizenship amendment on Michigan ballots for the midterm elections,” according to Courthouse News Service. “Americans for Citizen Voting asked the justices to intervene after the Michigan Board of State Canvassers invalidated its proposal” following the board’s determination that the proposal did not have enough valid signatures to be added to the ballot. Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied that request “without referring the appeal to the full court. He did not explain his decision.” Courthouse News Service noted that “Americans for Citizen Voting filed its emergency appeal at the U.S. Supreme Court just days before Michigan ballots were scheduled to be finalized on Friday.”

Mine safety commissioner fired by Trump gives up legal fight, citing Supreme Court

Zach Schonfeld, The Hill

In June, the Supreme Court expanded presidential firing power in Trump v. Slaughter, holding that the president has broad authority over approximately two dozen multi-member agencies that Congress intended to be independent. On Wednesday, Moshe Marvit cited that decision in announcing that he was dropping his lawsuit over President Donald Trump’s effort to remove him from the Federal Mine Safety and Health Review Commission. He said he “disagrees with the high court’s decision but conceded it means the agency is no longer independent,” according to The Hill. “Marvit is among a growing list of fired independent agency leaders who’ve thrown in the towel after the Supreme Court upended 91 years of precedent that had shielded them with firing protections.”

Trump administration aims to strip schools’ tax exemption if they consider race

Susan Svrluga and Danielle Douglas-Gabriel, The Washington Post

On Thursday, the IRS and Treasury Department announced plans to “eliminate tax-exempt status for any private school that discriminates ‘on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin in administration of its educational, admissions, scholarship, athletic, or other policies,’” escalating the Trump administration’s past efforts to prevent schools from considering race in admissions and other areas of campus life, according to The Washington Post. The administration argues that such consideration “violate[s] the law in the wake of a 2023 Supreme Court ruling banning the use of race-conscious admissions.” The new proposal “is subject to a lengthy public-comment period,” and would not go into effect until May 2027, at the earliest. “The agencies estimate that if it takes effect, the rule could affect as many as 18,000 primary and secondary schools, colleges, universities, professional schools, and trade schools.”

Democrats plot crackdown on Supreme Court

Susan Ferrechio, The Washington Times

During an event last weekend in Iowa, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who are poised to lead the Senate Judiciary Committee and House Judiciary Committee, respectively, if Democrats take control of the House and Senate in November, shared that they have monthly meetings on the future of the Supreme Court, at which they discuss “how they would police Supreme Court justices.” “Mr. Whitehouse and Mr. Raskin said they plan to issue subpoenas, which can be blocked by a filibuster in the Senate but not in the House,” according to The Washington Times. Whitehouse “did not specify who would be targeted with subpoenas, but noted that many questions remain regarding the court’s conservative justices. In particular, he pointed to Justice Clarence Thomas, who bought a $267,230 luxury motor coach using a loan from a wealthy healthcare executive that Senate investigators say was forgiven without repayment.”

On Site

Court News

Judge temporarily halts Trump’s latest birthright citizenship order

By Amy Howe

It has been just under a month since President Donald Trump issued a new executive order seeking to narrow the availability of birthright citizenship. On Wednesday, a federal judge in Maryland temporarily blocked the Trump administration from enforcing that order against an expansive group of children whose parents are in the United States temporarily or without proper documentation.

Court News

Sen. Jon Ossoff and other Democratic candidates urge justices to leave court ruling in place on political broadcasting rates

By Amy Howe

Four Democratic candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate urged the justices to leave in place a ruling by a federal appeals court that limited the availability of preferential advertising rates to candidates for political office. The candidates – former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who is running again in that state; Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running for reelection in Georgia; former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, who is running for Senate there; and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, who is running for reelection in Michigan – told the justices that “[n]o court has ever held, or even hinted,” that the preferential rates should be more broadly available.

Contributor Corner

Will the court consider due process rights for detained migrants?

By César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández

In his Immigration Matters column, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández explored Genalo v. Black, a case on whether the government can indefinitely detain long-term migrants who have been convicted of a variety of crimes without allowing them to ask an immigration judge for release on bond. The case is scheduled to be argued on Oct. 13, although recent developments might convince the court to remove it from its docket.

SCOTUS Outside Opinions

Court reform is liberal-coded nowadays. But it shouldn’t be.

By Gabe Roth

In a column for SCOTUSblog, Gabe Roth contended that “there’s nothing inherently partisan about court reform,” even if Democrats dominate the current discussion of potential changes to make to the Supreme Court. “Improving transparency and accountability in our historically opaque third branch – if done right – would not help one party or another,” Roth wrote.

Podcasts

Advisory Opinions

SCOTUS Majority Rules White House Ballroom Is A Go

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the 5-4 ballroom interim docket decision with Chief Justice John Roberts leading the dissenters, The New York Times’ piece on releasing the justices’ papers sooner rather than later, and a piece by Josh Morrow on AI in circuit decisions.

A Closer Look

Justice Henry Brockholst Livingston

Although Justia describes Henry Brockholst Livingston as having “spent all of his 16 years on the Court in the shadow of Chief Justice John Marshall, writing no memorable opinions,” another biography states that Livingston was the court’s “unofficial expert on commercial law until the arrival of Justice Story.” In any event, Livingston was certainly memorable in other ways – he survived an assassination attempt, killed a man in a duel, and had two “acts of dubious judicial decorum” involving John Quincy Adams and the case of Dartmouth College v. Woodward, respectively.

Livingston was born in New York City in November 1757 to a wealthy and influential family and raised in Elizabeth (then Elizabethtown), New Jersey. His father (for whom the town of Livingston, New Jersey, is named) later became governor of New Jersey. He graduated from the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University) in 1774 with James Madison as a classmate, enlisted in the Continental Army at 19, and was present when British General John Burgoyne surrendered at the Battle of Saratoga in October 1777. Livingston’s rank at the time is disputed: some sources say he was a captain, while others claim a lieutenant colonel. In 1779, he left for Spain as private secretary to his brother-in-law John Jay (yes, that John Jay), although the two were “often at odds.” On his way home three years later, Livingston was captured by the British and imprisoned in New York, although he was paroled after just three weeks as the war came to a close.

Admitted to the bar in 1783, Livingston served three terms in the state assembly and survived an assassination attempt in 1785. He also gave the first Fourth of July speech that was “in the presence of” President George Washington. Justice Joseph Story once described Livingston as having “an aquiline nose, high forehead, bold head, and projecting chin.” The first of those features played into a fatal duel in 1798 after Federalist James Jones tried to “wring [Livingston’s] nose” after Livingston insulted him. Livingston killed Jones, and although Livingston was not prosecuted, he reportedly “never fully recovered” psychologically following Jones’ death.

Livingston drifted into the Jeffersonian camp during the 1790s, and his work helping then-Vice President Thomas Jefferson win New York in 1800 got him a seat on the New York Supreme Court in 1802. In his four years there, Livingston wrote 149 opinions, most famously his dissent in the influential 1805 case of Pierson v. Post, where he argued that a hunter chasing a fox, not the passerby who kills it, has the better claim to the fox (law professor Josh Blackman has described this as the “definitive first year property case”).

Jefferson gave Livingston a recess appointment to Justice William Paterson’s seat in November 1806. The Senate confirmed him by voice vote in December, and he took the oath in January 1807. Used to writing separately in New York, Livingston fell in line with Marshall’s practice of a single opinion and had a relatively small output with only 38 majority opinions, eight dissents, and six concurrences in 16 years by one tally. Contemporaries knew him as “a silent observer” who calmed intra-justice tensions.

Although none of his Supreme Court opinions focused on major constitutional issues, many involved commercial law, such as disputes over notes, bills, and insurance policies. In 1818’s Dugan v. United States, he held that the federal government could enforce its contracts because “[i]t would be strange” to deny it “a right which is secured to every citizen of the United States.” Story, for his part, called him a “very able and independent judge.”

Livingston has also been remembered for less savory reasons, however. He apparently told then-counsel John Quincy Adams how 1810’s Fletcher v. Peck, the first time the Supreme Court held a state law unconstitutional, would come out before the court announced the decision, and in 1819’s Dartmouth College, his vote was reportedly influenced by extra-judicial conversations with Chancellor of New York and former colleague James Kent, who supported the majority’s position.

Livingston fell ill during the 1823 term and died in Washington at age 65. Justice Smith Thompson, nominated by President James Monroe, took Livingston’s seat on the court. Livingston’s death ended an 11-year period of an unchanged bench, then the longest such period in the Supreme Court’s history.

SCOTUS Quote

MR. KOERNER: “But if the shipment is done with the intent of avoiding taxes, which was contemplated by this statute –”

JUSTICE SCALIA: “That's not what it says. It makes it unlawful to knowingly ship it when they bear no evidence of payment of applicable taxes, and –”

MR. KOERNER: “– That's correct. There's a question of proof.”

JUSTICE SCALIA: “– there is no applicable taxes at the time that they ship it.”

MR. KOERNER: “But if you look at the legislative history, it was directly –”

JUSTICE SCALIA: “Oh, I don't look at legislative history.”

— Hemi Group LLC v. City of New York (2009)
